Barbara Jordan. The first Black woman elected to Congress from the South, representing Texas from 1973 to 1979. A commanding orator and constitutional scholar, she rose to national prominence during the Watergate hearings with moral gravity and rhetorical precision.

She was elected to the House from Houston in 1972 and took office in 1973. She served on the House Judiciary Committee, the first Black woman to do so, where she gained national fame during the Watergate impeachment inquiry in 1974. During the televised hearings, she delivered a principled speech on constitutional duty, declaring, "My faith in the Constitution is whole," as she grilled President Nixon's lawyers with judicial precision.

Before entering Congress, Jordan was a lawyer and Texas state legislator, bringing both legal expertise and moral authority to her legislative voice. She advocated for civil rights, voting rights enforcement, and environmental protection. She retired from Congress at age forty-two, citing health reasons, as she had multiple sclerosis. After leaving office, she became a revered teacher and public intellectual, lecturing at the University of Texas and remaining a symbol of integrity and eloquence in American public life.
